units.translation: O common benefit to mortals, having appeared.
Before some god appears as successor to your labors.
The heavenly dust, having appeared, persuades me.
Having appeared as an avenging spirit or an evil divinity from somewhere.
Master of masters, appear.
When the dark fire of good tidings appeared.
The dark one and the one behind, appearing white, near the halls.
To praise the favor before it has appeared.
For to those who appear well, may there be an addition of good.
But to your enemies I say that an avenger of you, father, should appear.
We have appeared as exactors of blood for him.
Saying that a double pollution has appeared from the city.
Or has this long-lived age appeared to the old?
Though they are unexpected, they will appear.
For my appearing well.
Will some Ethiopian woman appear?
And it has appeared to the descendants of those breathing bold Ares, greater than is just.
Or has he appeared as a teacher of every art to mortals?
Signs of my mind, that it sees something more than what has been revealed.
It seemed to me then that the best of the present circumstances was...
Perhaps I seem to you to be saying ancient things.
To us Hermes does not seem to speak unseasonably.
See now if these things seem helpful to you.
For to me now everything in my eyes appears full of fear, the opposite of the gods.
What is this that appears?
We would not appear to have done such great evils.
By such words I appeared to be wandering.
But when overcome, he will appear gentler.

Tzetzes spoke about the lengthened second syllable in Cramer's Anecdota Oxoniensia vol. 3 p. 358, 17. Similarly, Aeschylus lengthened the second syllable of the names Ιππομέδοντος [Hippomedon] and Παρθενοπαῖος [Parthenopaeus] for metrical necessity, about which we have spoken in their proper places.

phalerae (ornamental discs on horse trappings); in singular, the tip of the Persian king's tiara
in the plural they are called phalerae of horses, in the singular φάλαρον [phaleron] he called the tip of the Persian king's tiara

which Thomas Magister explains by τὴν ἐξοχήν [the prominence], with which can be compared the gloss of Hesychius φάλαρα: ἀστραγαλίσκος ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς περικεφαλαίας [phalerae: the small knob on the helmet]. Less correctly did the old scholiast understand it as the crest, φαίνων, δεικνύων τῆς περικεφαλαίας τὸν λόφον [showing, displaying the crest of the helmet].

In which sense Homer said εἰδόμενος [making oneself like] and εἰσάμενος [having made oneself like]: ἀπεικασθείς [having been made like] in a similar passage Euripides El. 979 ἆρ᾽ οὐκ ἀλάστωρ εἶπ᾽, ἀπεικασθεὶς θεῷ; [Did not an avenging spirit speak, having been made like a god?]
